scenes.headline: Consuming REST APIs with requests
scenes.subtitle: Fetching data over HTTP reliably
scenes.narration: A great many pipelines ingest their data from REST APIs, and the requests library makes those HTTP calls simple, readable, and easy to reason about.

scenes.headline: HTTP essentials
items: Headers carry auth and content type
scenes.narration: The HTTP verbs express intent: GET retrieves data while POST submits or creates it. Status codes tell you what happened, with the two hundreds meaning success, four hundreds signaling a client mistake, and five hundreds indicating a server failure. Headers carry metadata like authentication tokens and content type. And JSON is the payload format you'll encounter most often when working with modern APIs.

scenes.headline: A robust GET request
scenes.code:
import requests

resp = requests.get(
    'https://api.example.com/users',
    params={'page': 1},
    headers={'Authorization': f'Bearer {token}'},
    timeout=10,
)
resp.raise_for_status()
data = resp.json()
scenes.narration: This request passes query parameters, an authorization header carrying a bearer token, and crucially a timeout so the call can never hang forever. Calling raise_for_status converts any error status into an exception you can catch, rather than silently proceeding with a failed response. Only then do we parse the body with json, confident the request actually succeeded.

scenes.headline: Pagination loop
scenes.code:
results = []
url = 'https://api.example.com/items'
while url:
    r = requests.get(url, timeout=10)
    r.raise_for_status()
    body = r.json()
    results.extend(body['data'])
    url = body.get('next')
scenes.narration: Most APIs return large result sets in pages rather than all at once. This loop fetches a page, appends its records to the accumulator, and then reads the next-page link from the response. When the API stops providing a next link, url becomes None and the loop naturally ends, leaving you with the complete dataset.

scenes.headline: Production concerns
items: Reuse a Session for connection pooling
scenes.narration: A timeout on every call prevents a single slow endpoint from freezing your entire job. Retrying transient failures like a 429 rate limit or a 5xx server error, with exponential backoff between attempts, turns flaky endpoints into reliable ones. Respecting the rate limits the API advertises keeps you from being blocked. And reusing a Session object pools TCP connections, which is noticeably faster across many calls.

scenes.text: Always set timeout, call raise_for_status(), and retry transient errors with exponential backoff.
scenes.narration: Timeouts, status checks, and backoff retries are the three pillars that turn a fragile fetch script into dependable production ingestion.
